When choosing a mobility model for an outbreak analysis, we may be interested in
how well it explains the spread of infection between regions. A model can fit its
source mobility data closely yet give a different pattern of spread from another
plausible model. In this example we will compare those patterns using daily
incidence, so that both the timing of an outbreak and the number of infections
contribute to the comparison.

We will first construct a fictional set of regions and simulate an outbreak
using one of the bundled gravity models. We can then treat the daily new
infections from that simulation as our observations and ask how well different
mobility models reproduce them. Knowing which model generated the data makes
this a useful example for exploring the workflow, although a single simulated
outbreak cannot tell us which model would be appropriate for a real setting.

```{r setup}
library(nomad)
```

## A fictional place

Let's start with 24 hypothetical regions. Each has a name, population size and
location, giving us the inputs needed to predict a mobility matrix. We use
invented coordinates to construct pairwise distances in kilometres, rather than
trying to reproduce the geography of a particular country. The larger central
population and the smaller surrounding regions give the models a range of
population sizes and distances over which to predict movement.

```{r}
regions <- data.frame(
  region = c(
    "Central City", "North Market", "River East", "Hill West",
    "Airport", "Lake Town", "Copper Belt", "Forest Gate",
    "South Farms", "Old Mission", "Border Post", "Rail Junction",
    "Valley Clinic", "New Estate", "Quarry", "Harbour Road",
    "Sugar Plain", "Cattle Camp", "Highlands", "Mines End",
    "University", "Bus Depot", "Garden Ward", "Wetlands"
  ),
  x = c(
    0, 0.8, 1.6, -1.1, 2.5, -2.0, 3.1, -2.6,
    0.4, -1.8, 3.8, 1.9, -0.4, 0.9, 2.8, -3.1,
    -0.9, 1.4, -2.4, 3.5, 0.2, 1.1, -1.3, -2.8
  ),
  y = c(
    0, 1.2, -0.4, 0.9, 0.7, 2.2, 2.1, -0.1,
    -1.9, -2.4, -1.3, 1.8, 2.9, -0.9, -2.5, 1.1,
    -3.2, -2.8, 3.2, 3.0, 0.4, -1.6, 1.9, -1.7
  ),
  population = c(
    1250000, 260000, 340000, 180000, 410000, 120000,
    520000, 95000, 105000, 80000, 70000, 300000,
    65000, 220000, 90000, 140000, 75000, 55000,
    85000, 160000, 380000, 240000, 130000, 60000
  )
)

D <- as.matrix(dist(regions[, c("x", "y")])) * 70
dimnames(D) <- list(regions$region, regions$region)
N <- setNames(regions$population, regions$region)
newdata <- list(D = D, N = N)

regions[1:8, ]
```

The region names identify the rows and columns of `D` and the entries in `N`.
Keeping those names consistent lets us use the same inputs with each candidate
model and match the resulting predictions to the outbreak observations. For an
applied analysis, we would replace these invented inputs with distances and
population estimates for the study regions.

## Mobility candidates from `nomad`

We will compare normalised exponential gravity
(`zmb_fb_2025_mod_grav_exp_norm`) and exponential departure-diffusion
(`zmb_fb_2025_mod_dd_exp`), both fit to the Zambia Facebook dataset
`zmb_fb_2025`. These are the two models explored in
[Selecting a mobility model](selecting-a-model.html). Their parameters were
estimated from mobility observations. We will use the mean parameter estimates
to predict movement between our fictional regions and keep them fixed throughout
the outbreak comparison.

The gravity model will generate the example outbreak, while departure-diffusion
provides an alternative assumption about movement. We will also examine three
ensembles with gravity weights of 0.25, 0.5 and 0.75. The helper below produces
the corresponding matrix for any of these weights, with zero giving only
departure-diffusion and one giving only gravity.

```{r}
gravity_model <- model_db$zmb_fb_2025_mod_grav_exp_norm
diffusion_model <- model_db$zmb_fb_2025_mod_dd_exp

gravity_flows <- predict(gravity_model, newdata = newdata, unit = "km")
diffusion_flows <- predict(diffusion_model, newdata = newdata, unit = "km")

candidate_prediction <- function(weight_gravity) {
  if (weight_gravity == 0) {
    return(predict(diffusion_model, newdata = newdata, unit = "km"))
  }
  if (weight_gravity == 1) {
    return(predict(gravity_model, newdata = newdata, unit = "km"))
  }

  ensemble <- nomad_ensemble(
    list(diffusion = diffusion_model, gravity = gravity_model),
    weights = c(diffusion = 1 - weight_gravity, gravity = weight_gravity)
  )
  predict(ensemble, newdata = newdata, unit = "km")
}
```

## A spatially coupled SIR model

We use a stochastic susceptible-infectious-recovered (SIR) model with daily
updates. Infection spreads through contacts within each region and with other
regions, while infectious people recover and remain immune. The mobility matrix
determines how between-region contacts are distributed.

To obtain those contact shares, we remove within-region trips from the diagonal
and divide each row by its remaining total. An entry in `P` then gives the share
of an origin's outward movement going to a particular destination. We use these
shares to weight infectious prevalence in the destinations. This captures the
pattern of movement, without treating the source trip counts as daily journeys
or moving people between their home populations.

```{r coupling, fold=TRUE, fold_label="Show how to turn predicted flows into contact shares"}
flow_to_coupling <- function(M) {
  P <- as.matrix(M)
  diag(P) <- 0
  row_total <- rowSums(P)
  stopifnot(all(is.finite(P)), all(P >= 0), all(row_total > 0))
  P / row_total
}
```

The force of infection combines local prevalence with this weighted prevalence
in other regions,

$$
\lambda_i(t) = \beta\left[(1-\epsilon)\frac{I_i(t)}{N_i}
  + \epsilon\sum_j P_{ij}\frac{I_j(t)}{N_j}\right].
$$

Each day we draw new infections and recoveries from binomial distributions,
using probabilities $1-\exp[-\lambda_i(t)]$ and $1-\exp(-\gamma)$ respectively.
Both use the compartment sizes at the start of the day and preserve each
region's population.

For all candidates, we use a transmission rate `beta = 0.35` per day, a recovery
rate `gamma = 1 / 7` per day and a between-region mixing fraction `epsilon = 0.04`.
With daily updates, this gives an average infectious duration of about 7.5 days
and most exposure occurs locally. Starting with 60 infections in
Central City, we follow the outbreak for 120 days. Keeping these assumptions
the same lets us compare the effect of changing only the mobility model.

```{r sir, fold=TRUE, fold_label="Show the daily stochastic SIR simulation"}
simulate_sir <- function(P,
                         N,
                         days = 120,
                         beta = 0.35,
                         gamma = 1 / 7,
                         epsilon = 0.04,
                         seed_region = "Central City",
                         seed_infections = 60,
                         keep_history = FALSE) {
  S <- round(N)
  I <- setNames(rep(0, length(N)), names(N))
  R <- I
  I[seed_region] <- seed_infections
  S[seed_region] <- S[seed_region] - seed_infections

  incidence <- matrix(0, nrow = days, ncol = length(N),
                      dimnames = list(seq_len(days), names(N)))
  if (keep_history) history <- vector("list", days)
  p_recover <- 1 - exp(-gamma)

  for (day in seq_len(days)) {
    prevalence <- I / N
    imported <- as.numeric(P %*% prevalence)
    lambda <- beta * ((1 - epsilon) * prevalence + epsilon * imported)

    new_infections <- stats::rbinom(length(N), S, 1 - exp(-lambda))
    recoveries <- stats::rbinom(length(N), I, p_recover)
    S <- S - new_infections
    I <- I + new_infections - recoveries
    R <- R + recoveries
    incidence[day, ] <- new_infections

    if (keep_history) {
      history[[day]] <- data.frame(
        day = day, region = names(N), new_infections = new_infections,
        susceptible = S, infectious = I, recovered = R
      )
    }
  }

  if (keep_history) return(do.call(rbind, history))
  incidence
}

mean_sir <- function(P, N, days = 120, nsim = 80, seed = 1, ...) {
  set.seed(seed)
  total <- matrix(0, nrow = days, ncol = length(N),
                  dimnames = list(seq_len(days), names(N)))
  for (i in seq_len(nsim)) {
    total <- total + simulate_sir(P, N, days = days, ...)
  }
  total / nsim
}
```

The simulation returns daily new infections by region, or a fuller compartment
history when `keep_history = TRUE`. We use `mean_sir()` to average incidence over
80 runs per candidate. These runs capture random infection and recovery events
with the mobility and transmission parameters held fixed.

## Simulated outbreak data

We can now generate the observations using the gravity model. Setting a random
seed makes this particular outbreak reproducible when the vignette is run again.
The observed incidence consists of new infections during each day; the 60 people
already infectious at the start are an initial condition and are not counted as
new infections on day one.

```{r observations}
truth_coupling <- flow_to_coupling(gravity_flows)
set.seed(99)
observed_history <- simulate_sir(truth_coupling, N, keep_history = TRUE)
observed_incidence <- matrix(
  observed_history$new_infections, ncol = length(N), byrow = TRUE,
  dimnames = list(seq_len(120), names(N))
)
```

The panels below show how the same outbreak develops across all 24 regions.
Central City has infection from the start, whereas other regions must first
receive exposure through their connections to infected places. Their arrival
times and subsequent trajectories depend on those connections as well as on
random infection and recovery events. The panels share a time axis but have
separate vertical scales so that the smaller outbreaks remain visible. Use the
axis values when comparing numbers of infections between regions.

```{r regional-curves, fig.width=10, fig.height=9, fold=TRUE, fold_label="Show how to plot the regional outbreak curves", fig.alt="Daily incidence over 120 days in 24 fictional regions, generated with normalised exponential gravity fit to zmb_fb_2025"}
observed_history$region <- factor(observed_history$region, levels = regions$region)
ggplot2::ggplot(observed_history, ggplot2::aes(day, new_infections)) +
  ggplot2::geom_area(fill = "#33658a", alpha = 0.15) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(colour = "#33658a", linewidth = 0.45) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~region, ncol = 4, scales = "free_y") +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 40, 80, 120)) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "Day", y = "New infections",
    title = "Daily incidence in the simulated outbreak",
    subtitle = "Normalised exponential gravity fit to zmb_fb_2025",
    caption = "One stochastic SIR realisation; vertical scales differ between regions"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank(),
                 strip.text = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold"),
                 plot.title.position = "plot")
```

## Fit the mobility weight to daily incidence

We will compare five candidate weights, including the two individual models.
For each weight, we predict the mobility matrix, convert it to contact shares,
and run the same SIR model 80 times. We then compare the mean daily incidence
with the observations across all 120 days and all 24 regions. This retains
information about when cases occurred that would be lost by comparing only the
final outbreak size.

Our objective is the root mean squared difference between `log(1 + observed)`
and `log(1 + predicted)` daily incidence. The logarithm reduces the dominance of
the largest counts, allowing discrepancies in smaller outbreaks to contribute,
and adding one keeps days with no cases in the comparison. Every region-day
pair has equal weight on this transformed scale. We do not rescale predictions
to match the observed total, shift their timing, or adjust any transmission
parameters to improve a candidate's score.

We choose the weight with the smallest error from the five values we tried.
This gives a simple grid search for the best match to the observed incidence.
The scores rank these candidates for this outbreak, but do not give probabilities
that the models are correct or an uncertainty interval for the selected weight.

```{r scores, fold=TRUE, fold_label="Show how to score each candidate against daily incidence"}
log_rmse <- function(observed, predicted) {
  stopifnot(identical(dimnames(observed), dimnames(predicted)))
  sqrt(mean((log1p(observed) - log1p(predicted))^2))
}

score_candidate <- function(weight_gravity, nsim = 80, seed = 1000) {
  flows <- candidate_prediction(weight_gravity)
  predicted <- mean_sir(
    flow_to_coupling(flows), N, nsim = nsim,
    seed = seed + round(100 * weight_gravity)
  )
  list(
    prediction = predicted,
    score = data.frame(
      weight_gravity = weight_gravity,
      weight_departure = 1 - weight_gravity,
      log_RMSE = log_rmse(observed_incidence, predicted)
    )
  )
}

weights <- c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1)
candidate_results <- lapply(weights, score_candidate)
scores <- do.call(rbind, lapply(candidate_results, `[[`, "score"))
scores <- scores[order(scores$log_RMSE), ]
rownames(scores) <- NULL
knitr::kable(
  scores, digits = 3,
  col.names = c("Gravity weight", "Departure-diffusion weight", "Daily log RMSE"),
  caption = paste("Normalised exponential gravity and exponential departure-diffusion",
                  "fit to zmb_fb_2025; scored against the synthetic daily incidence")
)
```

The lowest score in this run occurs at a gravity weight of
`r scores$weight_gravity[1]`. Although gravity generated the observations, the
observed outbreak is only one stochastic realisation, so its trajectory will
differ from the mean over repeated simulations. A nearby ensemble can sometimes
score better for that reason. The candidate means also vary between batches of simulations because each is
estimated from a finite number of runs. If scores are close,
we would want to repeat the calculation with more simulations and different
seeds before treating their ordering as meaningful.

## Compare observed and predicted incidence

The scatter plot below compares observed daily incidence with the mean predicted
incidence for gravity, departure-diffusion and the best intermediate ensemble.
That ensemble is the mixture with the lowest score among the three weights
between zero and one. Each point is one region on one day, with points above the diagonal indicating
overprediction and points below it indicating underprediction. All three panels
use the same log(1 + incidence) scales so that small counts and days with no
infections are visible alongside the largest counts.

```{r comparison-data, fold=TRUE, fold_label="Show how to assemble the observed and predicted daily incidence"}
prediction_by_weight <- setNames(
  lapply(candidate_results, `[[`, "prediction"), weights
)
best_ensemble_weight <- scores$weight_gravity[
  scores$weight_gravity > 0 & scores$weight_gravity < 1
][1]
comparison_weights <- c(1, best_ensemble_weight, 0)
comparison_labels <- c(
  "Gravity", paste0(100 * best_ensemble_weight, "% gravity ensemble"),
  "Departure-diffusion"
)
comparison <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(comparison_weights), function(i) {
  predicted <- prediction_by_weight[[as.character(comparison_weights[i])]]
  out <- observed_history[, c("day", "region", "new_infections")]
  out$predicted <- as.vector(t(predicted))
  out$model <- comparison_labels[i]
  out$log_difference <- log1p(out$predicted) - log1p(out$new_infections)
  out
}))
comparison$model <- factor(comparison$model, levels = comparison_labels)
```

```{r incidence-scatter, fig.width=10, fig.height=4.3, fold=TRUE, fold_label="Show how to compare observed and predicted daily incidence", fig.alt="Observed versus predicted daily incidence for gravity, departure-diffusion and the best intermediate ensemble, using models fit to zmb_fb_2025; each point is one region-day"}
limit <- max(comparison$new_infections, comparison$predicted)
axis_labels <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
ggplot2::ggplot(comparison, ggplot2::aes(new_infections, predicted, colour = model)) +
  ggplot2::geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey35") +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 0.7, alpha = 0.18) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~model, nrow = 1) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = c("#2166ac", "#e08214", "#b2182b")) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(
    trans = "log1p", limits = c(0, limit), breaks = c(0, 10, 100, 1000, 10000),
    labels = axis_labels
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(
    trans = "log1p", limits = c(0, limit), breaks = c(0, 10, 100, 1000, 10000),
    labels = axis_labels
  ) +
  ggplot2::coord_fixed() +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "Observed daily new infections", y = "Predicted daily new infections",
    title = "Observed and predicted daily incidence",
    subtitle = "Normalised exponential gravity and exponential departure-diffusion fit to zmb_fb_2025",
    caption = "Each point is one region-day; predictions are means of 80 SIR runs per candidate."
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "none", panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank(),
                 strip.text = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold"),
                 plot.title.position = "plot")
```

The scatter plot makes overall agreement easy to see, but does not show where
or when the differences occur. The heatmap below retains that information,
showing the signed log difference for each region and day. Red means predicted
incidence is higher than observed, while blue means it is lower. A run of red
followed by blue can suggest that a predicted outbreak is too early. Some
variation remains even for the generating model, because we are comparing
simulation averages with one stochastic outbreak.

```{r daily-residuals, fig.width=10, fig.height=10, fold=TRUE, fold_label="Show how to plot daily incidence differences", fig.alt="Region-by-day log incidence differences for three candidates based on the zmb_fb_2025 gravity and departure-diffusion fits"}
comparison$region <- factor(comparison$region, levels = rev(regions$region))
limit <- max(abs(comparison$log_difference))
ggplot2::ggplot(comparison, ggplot2::aes(day, region, fill = log_difference)) +
  ggplot2::geom_tile() +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~model, ncol = 1) +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b",
    midpoint = 0, limits = c(-limit, limit)
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_discrete(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "Day", y = NULL, fill = "log(1 + predicted) - log(1 + observed)",
    title = "Daily incidence differences by region",
    subtitle = "Normalised exponential gravity and exponential departure-diffusion fit to zmb_fb_2025"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid = ggplot2::element_blank(),
                 strip.text = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold"),
                 plot.title.position = "plot")
```

## Using this approach in an analysis

This example compares mobility assumptions while holding everything else fixed.
It helps us see whether a change in the predicted pattern of travel changes the
daily incidence in places we care about. The selected weight is specific to this
simulated outbreak, the contact model, and the five values we tried. Since the
same outbreak is used for both choosing the weight and assessing its fit, the
results show how well the candidates explain these observations. They do not
yet show how well the selected model would predict a different outbreak or a
later period that was not used to choose the weight.

In a real analysis, transmission rates, initial infections and the relationship
between infections and recorded cases would also need justification. Changes in
those assumptions could compensate for differences between mobility models,
making the mobility weight difficult to identify from case data alone. The
simulation averages here include infection and recovery randomness, but do not
propagate uncertainty in mobility parameters, population sizes or transmission
parameters. Before using a fitted weight to make forecasts, we would need to
examine those sources of uncertainty and assess predictions against data that
were not used to choose the weight.
